newsitem.title: CHINA: HK human rights group condemns Tung election plan.
newsitem.headline: HK human rights group condemns Tung election plan.

text.p: Human rights activists in Hong Kong on Thursday slammed the new China-anointed government's electoral plans as unfair.
The Hong Kong Human Rights Monitor group urged leader Tung Chee-hwa's government to speed up democratisation by amending the territory's constitution, the Basic Law.
The attack was made on the last day of a pulse-taking exercise launched by Tung last week to consult the public on the planned arrangements for next May's legislative elections.
"These changes will make the functional constituencies elections secret, unfair and dishonest," said lawyer Paul Harris, the chairman and spokesman of the human rights group.

China scrapped Hong Kong's colonial elected legislature when it resumed sovereignty over the territory on July 1, and replaced it with a Beijing-appointed provisional chamber which operates until a new legislature is elected next year.
Under Tung's proposal, half of the 60 seats of the coming Legislative Council will be filled by representatives from business and professional bodies in so-called functional constituencies.
Twenty seats are to be returned by geographical constituencies and 10 by an election committee made up of businessmen and professionals.

Harris said the proposal to give votes in functional constituencies to corporations rather than individuals, which would mean a cut in the voting population and more powers for business, was a roll-back of democracy that breached the Basic Law.
"It is very much open to legal challenge," he said. However, his group is not planning any legal action because it does not have the funds.
The Basic Law stipulates that democratisation should be advanced gradually and in orderly fashion.

For functional constituencies, more than two million people who were eligible to vote in the 1995 Legislative Council polls would be disenfranchised under Tung's proposal. They would be replaced by corporate votes adding up to no more than 10,000 ballots.
Harris said such a "small circle election" would "foster corruption".

The human rights activist and lawyer also said the territory of 6.4 million people was mature enough to proceed to fully democratic elections in 1998 and that the Basic Law should be changed to allow such polls.
"We believe Hong Kong society is a mature society...and that Hong Kong people can responsibly exercise their democratic rights," Harris said.
The post-colonial constitution sets out a timetable for the 60-seat legislature to be elected through geographical constituencies, which would be in 2047.
The group blasted the nine-day consultation exercise as a sham. "I don't call that a consultation. That's simply notifying what you are going to do," Harris said.
He said Tung should understand that social tensions would arise if the people had no voice in the legislature in the event that Hong Kong is hit by an economic downturn.

Under the planned electoral arrangements, Hong Kong will be divided into five geographical constituencies each with three to five seats. This contrasts with arrangements in the 1995 election where the territory was divided into 20 smaller geographical constituencies, each with one seat.
The popular Democratic Party has criticised the change as favouring less popular parties.
Hong Kong returned to China on July 1 after 156 years of British rule.
